title: Enkidu speaks to the Gate
short: Thompson places Enkidu's address to a great wooden door here; modern editions put it in Tablet VII, where the dying Enkidu curses the door he made from the cedar.
body: In George's edition this speech belongs to Tablet VII: Enkidu, sick and dying, addresses the door he made for Enlil's temple at Nippur from the tallest cedar of the forest, regretting that he gave it to a god who now wants his death. Thompson, lacking the context, took it as the 'Gate of the Forest' reached before the fight. The admiration of the wood, the measurements and the mention of Nippur all fit George's reading better. This is one of the clearest cases in which modern knowledge rearranges Thompson's text.

title: Leagues (beru)
short: The 'league' renders beru, a 'double-hour' of travel (about 10 km): journey distances in the epic are measured in time.
body: The beru was both a unit of time (two hours) and the distance walked in that time. Tablet IV in George's edition repeats a formula for each stage: at twenty leagues they broke bread, at thirty they made camp, covering fifty leagues a day, a journey of a month and a half in three days. Thompson's 'fortieth league' and 'sixtieth' (V) and his 'fortieth hour' and 'sixtieth' (XI) reflect the same formula, read as hours rather than double-hours.

title: The gar (rod)
short: The gar was a measure of length of about 6 metres: the door is about 36 m high and 12 m wide.
body: Thompson leaves the Sumerian unit untranslated; George renders 'rod'. Such measurements, impossibly large for a real door, emphasise the magnificence of the cedar. The same unit gives the dimensions of Uta-Napishtim's ark (ten gar each way, XI) and of Gilgamish's punting poles (five gar each, X). Thompson keeps such Babylonian units throughout (gar, shar, talent, mana), which gives his version an archaic texture but needs glossing for the modern reader.

title: Nippur, city of Enlil
short: Nippur, in central Babylonia, was the holy city of Enlil and the religious centre of Sumer.
body: Enlil's temple Ekur stood at Nippur; kings sent precious materials there to win the god's favour. In George's reading the heroes float a great cedar door down the Euphrates to Nippur at the end of Tablet V. Thompson's note records a correction in his Addenda for this line. Gilgamish goes to Ekur to plead for Enkidu in Tablet XII. Thompson's idea that the gate was made in Nippur reflects his placing of the scene.

title: Humbaba's seven garments (auras)
short: The 'seven garments' Humbaba can put on are his seven auras of terror, divine radiance worn like cloaks.
body: In Mesopotamian belief gods and monsters wore 'radiance' (melemmu) and 'terror' (puluhtu) as garments of light. In the Sumerian 'Bilgames and Huwawa' the hero tricks Huwawa into giving up his seven auras one by one. In the Akkadian texts the friends hurry to attack before he can put all of them on. Thompson's broken lines ('Thou shall put on seven garments ... putting on, and six') preserve this motif without explaining it.

title: Enkidu's twelve-day illness
short: Thompson places Enkidu's twelve-day illness before the fight; modern editions put it at his deathbed in Tablet VII.
body: In George's edition this count of days belongs to the end of Tablet VII, when Enkidu lies dying after the gods' sentence: the days are counted one by one up to the twelfth. Thompson's arrangement, made before this was clear, has Enkidu fall sick and recover before the Cedar Forest. Read in its modern place the passage shows the slow approach of death, with Enkidu lamenting that he does not die gloriously in battle.

title: Enkidu's fear and Gilgamish's encouragement
short: On the threshold of the forest Enkidu's arms go weak and Gilgamish now encourages him: the roles of the friends reverse.
body: Earlier Enkidu was the one who warned and knew the way. Now Gilgamish repeats the elders' proverb and urges him to 'forget death'. Such alternation of fear and courage between the two friends is a structure George traces through Tablets IV-V. The words 'stricken with palsy' render a phrase for limbs losing strength, the standard Akkadian description of fear. The exchange also reflects Thompson's arrangement, since he believed Enkidu had just recovered from an illness.

title: 'Forget death'
short: Gilgamish urges Enkidu to 'forget death': the heroic ethic that the poem will later test.
body: At this stage Gilgamish believes that fear of death can simply be set aside for the sake of glory. After Enkidu's death he will be unable to forget it; 'death is wherever I listen' (XI). The phrase therefore marks the distance the hero will travel. Compare his earlier speech: 'Who, O my friend, is unconquer'd by [death]?' (III). The young king's confidence is sincere but untested; the poem lets the reader see how hollow it will sound after Enkidu's death.
